analysis.one_liner: Creates a government-funded jobs guarantee paid for by a tax on stock and bond trades.
analysis.headline: The bill never received a hearing or vote, dying in committee with zero cosponsors from either party in the 116th Congress.
analysis.plain_summary: The Jobs for All Act would create a National Full Employment Trust Fund to guarantee a job to anyone who wants one, with grants to states, cities, and nonprofits for public work like affordable housing, school repair, childcare, parks, and emergency food programs. The fund would be paid for by a new tax on securities trades — 0.2% on stocks and 0.06% on bonds and derivatives — plus, if needed, loans from the Federal Reserve when unemployment rises. Program jobs would pay wages comparable to what public-sector employees earn for similar work in the same community, and the bill bars employers from using program workers to replace laid-off staff or undercut union jobs.
analysis.who_benefits: Unemployed and involuntarily part-time workers, who could get certified at a local job center and placed in a full-time, publicly funded job at community-standard pay with benefits, plus training if they need it. Communities with high poverty and foreclosures would get housing, school, park, and childcare projects staffed by these workers. At least 35% of jobs would go to people identified as disadvantaged, and priority would go to the areas with the worst economic need.

how_it_helps.text: Creates a National Full Employment Trust Fund administered by the Department of Labor to fund jobs and free-standing training programs, aiming for full employment as a matter of federal policy.

Grants fund affordable housing construction and repair, childcare and health services, youth employment, school and park repair, emergency food programs, Head Start staffing, environmental work, and WPA-style arts and culture jobs.
Program workers earn pay and benefits comparable to local public-sector employees doing similar work, and construction workers must receive local prevailing wages.

Employers receiving funds cannot lay off or reduce the hours or benefits of existing employees to make room for program hires, and cannot fill positions that would undercut workers under a collective bargaining agreement without union consent.
Priority goes to areas with the highest unemployment, poverty, concentrated poverty, foreclosure rates, and poor health indicators, and at least 35% of jobs must go to disadvantaged individuals.

Program employees remain registered as job-seekers and get paid time off to interview for private-sector jobs, so the program is designed as a bridge, not a trap; refusing a suitable private job without good cause costs 30 days of eligibility.

analysis.who_pays: Investors and trading firms pay a new federal tax on securities transactions: 0.2% of the value of each stock trade and 0.06% on bonds and derivatives, collected from exchanges and brokers. Because trading firms could pass some of this cost along in fees, ordinary people with 401(k)s and brokerage accounts could bear part of it, though purchases of mutual fund shares are explicitly exempt. The bill also obligates the Federal Reserve to lend to the trust fund whenever unemployment would otherwise rise more than one percentage point.

drawbacks.text: The trading tax applies to any purchase by or involving a U.S. person, including individual investors' stock and bond purchases, and trading firms can be expected to pass tax costs into the fees and spreads ordinary savers pay; only mutual fund purchases, initial stock issuances, and very short-term debt are exempt.

The bill requires the Federal Reserve to lend the trust fund whatever is needed to keep unemployment from rising more than one percentage point, which would draw the central bank directly into fiscal job-creation decisions it historically has not made.

A standing federal job guarantee with prevailing public-sector wages is an open-ended spending commitment with no stated total cost, and the CRS summary and bill text provide no fiscal estimate of the program's size.

The bill's funding depends on trading volume, so a sustained drop in market activity would shrink the fund's revenue while unemployment-related job demand rises, a mismatch only the Federal Reserve lending mandate would paper over.

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: The core benefit — a guaranteed job at decent wages for anyone who wants one, producing public goods like housing and childcare while outlawing displacement of existing workers — is large and directly aimed at ordinary people. The cost is a tax concentrated on securities trading, which falls hardest on high-volume traders but would also slightly raise costs for ordinary investors, and the program's total price tag is unestimated. The Fed lending mandate is the most questionable design feature, effectively making the central bank the funder of last resort for federal job creation. Honest supporters would have to acknowledge the scale and cost uncertainty; the trade-off is a real public benefit bought with a real, if narrow, tax on finance.

outcome.mechanism: It was referred to the Education and Labor and Ways and Means committees the day it was introduced, and neither committee ever held a hearing or markup, so it died there when the Congress ended in January 2021.

narrative.text: Rep. Frederica Wilson introduced the bill on February 6, 2019, and it was referred to the House Committee on Education and Labor and the Committee on Ways and Means.
No other member of the House signed on as a cosponsor — the bill had zero cosponsors for its entire two-year run.
The committees took no further action: no hearing, no markup, and no floor vote appears in the complete action history.
Because the 116th Congress ended on January 3, 2021 without the bill advancing, the bill is dead and would have to be reintroduced from scratch in a new Congress.

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: Securities trading firms and their largest clients are better off, since no trading tax was ever enacted; no worker gained a program job.

analysis.who_came_out_ahead_short: Securities traders who avoided the tax

for.name: Rep. Frederica S. Wilson
for.what_they_did: Introduced the Jobs for All Act and sponsored it; the bill drew no other cosponsors during the entire Congress.

against.name: Rep. Bobby Scott
against.role: Chair, House Education and Labor Committee
against.what_they_did: His committee received the referral on the day of introduction and never held a hearing or markup on the bill.

against.name: Rep. Richard Neal
against.role: Chair, House Ways and Means Committee
against.what_they_did: His committee, which had jurisdiction over the bill's securities transaction tax, received the referral and never took action on it.

sides.party_line_note: No vote was ever taken, so party positions on the merits are unknown, but the bill attracted zero cosponsors from either party — not even from the 230 other House Democrats.

industries.note: The bill would tax every covered stock trade at 0.2% and bond and derivative trades at 0.06%, collected by exchanges and brokers, to fund the job guarantee. High-frequency and large institutional traders bear the heaviest cost; retail investors could see some of it passed through in fees, though mutual fund purchases are exempt.

industries.industry: State and local governments and nonprofits
industries.note: They are the eligible grant recipients and would receive federal money to hire workers for housing, schools, parks, childcare, and food programs they already struggle to fund.

They gain a new funding stream and workforce, but the bill bars them from using program workers to displace existing employees, lay off workers to make room, or fill union-covered positions without union consent, and requires paying prevailing public-sector wages.
